intro: Every system ran the same scenarios, one after another, against a fresh PostgreSQL 18.6 cluster capped at 4 CPUs, on one host. Each section says what it asks, how it was run, and what to watch for when reading it. Absolute numbers depend on this host; the comparisons within a section are the point.

contracts.label: Job frameworks
contracts.text: A job is claimed by one worker, retried with backoff and completed or failed individually.

contracts.label: Durable workflow
contracts.text: Tasks run as checkpointed steps that replay after an interruption; driven here as one-step jobs through its worker.

contracts.label: Visibility queue
contracts.text: A message becomes invisible when read and reappears unless deleted; no per-job retry policy, scheduling or dead-letter handling beyond its archive.

contracts.label: Event queue (PgQ lineage)
contracts.text: Consumers read batches cut by a ticker and acknowledge a whole batch in one statement. Driven here as competing consumers; batch acknowledgement is a lighter contract than per-job completion.

sections.title: Throughput at saturation
sections.question: How many 1 ms jobs per second does one worker process complete as it gets more workers?
sections.setup: Out of the box: the producer keeps 4,000 jobs queued; one worker process with 4, 16, 64 or 128 workers and a pool of workers + 8 connections; 30 s warmup, then 150 s measured. Tuned: each system at the settings its own documentation points to, within one budget for all: at most 4 processes, 128 handlers and 200 connections, the same 1 ms jobs, measured at one queue and at its recommended number of queues.
read: PgQue and PGMQ provide lighter contracts than the job frameworks; compare them with each other, not with job frameworks.
Queue wait dominates claim latency here by design, so throughput is the figure to compare.
The tuned settings are listed below with their sources in each system's proposal; corrections from maintainers are welcome.

sections.title: Latency at a steady 800 jobs/s
sections.question: At a rate every system should sustain, how quickly does a job go from insert to completion?
sections.setup: 800 jobs/s offered, 32 workers, one process; 60 s warmup, then 300 s measured.
read: A system that cannot keep up builds a backlog, and its latency grows for the whole run; those are marked with the rate they reached.

charts.title: Pickup latency, p99
charts.caption: Insert to a worker starting the job.

sections.title: Cost of doing nothing
sections.question: With workers running and no jobs, how much does each system cost the database?
sections.setup: One process with 8 workers after a short warmup; 10 minutes with nothing enqueued.
read: Background polling, heartbeats and maintenance all show up here; they are paid on every deployment, busy or not.

charts.title: Postgres private memory while idle
charts.caption: Backend-local memory in the Postgres container (shared buffers excluded).

sections.title: PostgreSQL restart under load
sections.question: When the database restarts mid-run, does the system come back and work off what accumulated?
sections.setup: Two processes, 400 jobs/s each, 16 workers each. 90 s baseline; Postgres stopped for 45 s and started again; 120 s recovery.
read: Awa, Oban, pg-boss and River reconnect inside the running worker. PGMQ and PgQue are consumed by the adapters’ own loops, which reconnect.

Absurd's Python worker loop and Procrastinate's worker both stop when they lose the database, and expect a process supervisor (systemd, Kubernetes) to start them again. Their adapters restart the worker after 1 s, as a supervisor would. Without a supervisor, these workers stay stopped.
Zero after the restart means no jobs completed for the rest of the run.

sections.title: Impact on a neighbouring application
sections.question: Does a busy queue slow down unrelated transactions on the same server?
sections.setup: pgbench runs a TPC-B-like workload at a fixed 300 TPS on a separate database throughout. The queue runs at 0, 400, 1,600, then 400 jobs/s.
read: Latency is measured from each pgbench transaction's scheduled start, so it includes any queueing.

sections.title: Logical replication alongside the queue
sections.question: Does the queue coexist with CDC on the same database, including when the CDC consumer stops?
sections.setup: A FOR ALL TABLES publication, a pgoutput slot and a streaming consumer; 400 jobs/s. The consumer is frozen for 4 minutes, then resumes.
read: A table without a replica identity rejects UPDATE and DELETE while a FOR ALL TABLES publication exists.
Dead catalog tuples pile up when a system creates or truncates tables while a stalled slot holds back catalog cleanup.

sections.title: A herd of scheduled jobs
sections.question: When 20,000 jobs come due at the same instant, how late do they start, and do immediate jobs suffer?
sections.setup: 20,000 jobs scheduled for one instant while a 200 jobs/s stream of immediate jobs keeps flowing; 16 workers.
read: PgQue has no delayed delivery and is omitted from the herd figures.

sections.title: A storm of failing jobs
sections.question: When a third of jobs start failing, does useful work keep flowing?
sections.setup: 200 jobs/s, 16 workers. For 6 minutes 30% of new jobs fail once and 1% always fail; at most 5 attempts; each system's own backoff applies.
read: Backoff policies differ by orders of magnitude between systems; that difference is part of what this measures.

sections.title: Many queues
sections.question: What does spreading the same load over 200 queues cost, and how does each system serve many queues?
sections.setup: One process. 200 jobs/s in total, round-robin over 1 queue and then over 200 queues (1 job/s per queue); 16 handlers and 24 connections requested; each system uses its own idiomatic way of serving many queues, the same in both runs; 4 minutes busy, then 3 minutes idle.
read: Awa (weighted workers), Procrastinate (one worker over every queue), PGMQ and PgQue share 16 handlers across all 200 queues.
River, Oban, pg-boss and Absurd need at least one worker per queue, so they run 200 at 200 queues. That is part of the result.
Per-queue polling and listening connections multiply with the queue count.

rows.text: One client per queue (200 handler slots), sharing 16 connections; 250 ms poll (the SDK default).
Weighted mode: one pool of 16 workers across every queue; one LISTEN connection.

sections.title: Large job arguments
sections.question: What happens with 64 KiB and 1 MiB arguments, and does the database shrink back afterwards?
sections.setup: Incompressible arguments. Saturation: one process, 64 workers, 2,000 jobs queued, 120 s. Backlog: about 8 GiB of 1 MiB jobs preloaded by four processes, then drained by 4 × 16 workers.
read: The saturation cells are bound by one producer connection, so they compare insert paths as much as workers.
PostgreSQL keeps a table's disk space after its rows are deleted; only systems that truncate or drop storage give it back without VACUUM FULL.

sections.question: At a gentle rate with 64 KiB arguments, how much WAL is written and how much space is left behind?
sections.setup: 64 KiB incompressible arguments at 50 jobs/s for 5 minutes, then 3 minutes of draining.

sections.title: Long-running jobs
sections.question: What does it cost to keep jobs running for 40 seconds each?
sections.setup: Two processes × 100 workers; 40 s jobs; 150 held, then a steady stream for 6 minutes.
read: Heartbeats and lease extensions are writes. A timeout shorter than the job causes duplicate execution.

sections.title: Draining a backlog
sections.question: How fast does a 200,000-job backlog drain, and how big is the database afterwards?
sections.setup: 200,000 jobs preloaded behind a gate, then drained by 64 workers, then 4 minutes idle.

sections.title: A million abandoned claims
sections.question: When an entire fleet dies holding about a million claimed jobs, how long until those jobs have run?
sections.setup: Four processes preload 1,000,000 jobs and claim them all while their handlers hold instead of running. All four are killed at once (SIGKILL); a fresh fleet of 4 × 128 workers starts, with 80 new jobs/s arriving. Every claim timeout is 300 s.
read: Timeout-based systems cannot release a claim before its timeout, which has to exceed the longest job; the first rescue is mostly configuration. The rate after that is the system.

PgQue is a different contract, not a faster rescue. A consumer's claim is one open batch (here about 200,000 events each). The restarted consumer gets the same batch back at once, reads it in one query, runs the handlers and acknowledges the whole batch with one statement. The job frameworks write a state change for every one of the million jobs.
The completion curves include working the jobs off again, so the fresh fleet's speed bounds them.
